questionText: What is the .NET Generic Host, and what does Host.CreateApplicationBuilder set up for you?
shortAnswer: The Generic Host standardizes app startup: configuration (JSON/env/args), logging (Serilog/console), DI container, hosted services, and lifetime management in a few lines. CreateApplicationBuilder wires all defaults — you add services, build, and run.
detailedAnswer: Before: every app hand-rolled ConfigurationBuilder + ServiceCollection + LoggerFactory + manual lifetime (inconsistent, untested composition). Host.CreateApplicationBuilder gives: layered configuration (appsettings/env/args/secrets), logging providers, the DI container with validation hooks, IHostEnvironment (Development/Staging/Production branching), lifetime (ApplicationStarted/Stopping/Stopped tokens), and hosted-service orchestration. Our WPF App and Api Program both follow it (same pattern, UI and server). Customization: ConfigureHostConfiguration/ConfigureAppConfiguration (extra sources: Key Vault, YAML), ConfigureServices (all registrations), ConfigureLogging (Serilog), UseConsoleLifetime (Ctrl+C), UseWindowsService/UseSystemd (OS integration — content root + lifetime wiring in one call). Testing: build the host in tests (composition test), override services (doubles), run hosted services selectively. Anti-patterns: multiple hosts per process (one host owns lifetime), business logic in Program.cs (move to services), and reading config before Build without validation (ValidateOnStart).
internalWorking: Build compiles the service descriptors into the provider (validates with options), starts hosted services in registration order (StartAsync each), then blocks on the lifetime wait handle (ConsoleLifetime binds Ctrl+C/SIGTERM to ApplicationStopping). StopAsync reverses (bounded by ShutdownTimeout).
realWorldUsage: APIs, workers, Windows services, systemd daemons, and our own Api + WPF hosts.
commonMistake: Logic in Program.cs (untestable — move to services), hand-rolled configuration (inconsistent layering), and new Host per test without disposal (slow suites — fixture hosts).
technicalConversation: Ask what their Main does — host-build-run with thin wiring (mature) versus pages of manual setup (debt).
interviewFollowUp: What does the host own that individual libraries should never own themselves?
keyTakeaway: One host per app owns config, logging, DI, services, and lifetime. Thin Program, fat services.

questionText: What is the difference between IHostedService and BackgroundService, and which should you implement?
shortAnswer: IHostedService is the interface (StartAsync/StopAsync) — implement for event-driven or custom lifecycles. BackgroundService is the base class implementing it for the common long-running ExecuteAsync loop — inherit for 95% of workers (timers, consumers, relays).
detailedAnswer: IHostedService: StartAsync(CancellationToken) (called at host start — must return promptly; long work goes to background tasks, never block it), StopAsync (graceful stop, bounded by ShutdownTimeout). Implement directly for: listeners needing custom start/stop choreography (socket accept loops with explicit bind/unbind), composite services starting children in order, or wrappers around non-Task lifecycles. BackgroundService: implements the interface with ExecuteAsync(stoppingToken) running as a managed Task + StopAsync awaiting it (with timeout semantics) — inherit for loops/consumers/relays (our OutboxRelay pattern). Rules shared: singleton-only ctor deps, scopes per unit of work, honor the token everywhere, per-item try/catch (poison must not kill the host), no async void. Multiple hosted services start in registration order (no dependencies between them — readiness probes coordinate). Testing: BackgroundService logic via direct ExecuteAsync calls with fakes (no host needed for unit scope); IHostedService customs need start/stop sequence tests. Registration: AddHostedService<T> (singleton lifetime enforced).
internalWorking: Host calls StartAsync sequentially (each must complete fast — BackgroundService's returns after launching ExecuteAsync as a Task); StopAsync signals cancellation then awaits the task (ShutdownTimeout bounds it). Exceptions in ExecuteAsync surface via the task (unobserved → host process exit in modern .NET — hence per-item catches).
realWorldUsage: Pollers, queue consumers, cache warmers, file watchers, and scheduled syncs.
commonMistake: Blocking StartAsync (host never finishes starting), scoped ctor deps (captive — factories/scopes), fire-and-forget Tasks (unobserved death), and StopAsync that doesn't actually stop work (shutdown hangs to timeout).
technicalConversation: Ask how their workers get fresh DbContexts per tick — scope-per-iteration (correct) versus injected-scoped (captive) is the review line.
interviewFollowUp: Why must StartAsync return promptly, and what happens to the host if it doesn't?
keyTakeaway: Interface for custom lifecycles, base class for loops. Singleton ctor, scoped work, token everywhere.

questionText: How does graceful shutdown work in .NET (SIGTERM, CancellationToken, draining)?
shortAnswer: SIGTERM/Ctrl+C cancels ApplicationStopping → stoppingTokens fire → hosted services drain (finish in-flight, stop accepting) within ShutdownTimeout (default 5s) → host exits. Design for it: pass tokens everywhere, checkpoint progress, make work idempotent so kills are safe.
detailedAnswer: Sequence: orchestrator sends SIGTERM → ConsoleLifetime triggers ApplicationStopping → ExecuteAsync loops observe cancellation → StopAsync runs per service (drain: complete channels, flush batches, checkpoint offsets) → ApplicationStopped → process exits (SIGKILL after grace, e.g. K8s terminationGracePeriodSeconds). Design rules: (1) Tokens into every await (delays, HTTP, DB, channel reads — a single non-cancellable await hangs shutdown to timeout). (2) Drain, don't abort: stop accepting new work first (Channel.Writer.Complete / stop polling), finish in-flight with a bounded drain timeout, then exit. (3) Checkpoint: persist offsets/cursors per batch (restart resumes, not restarts). (4) Idempotency: assume kills mid-batch (at-least-once + idempotent appliers = safe restarts). (5) Timeouts: ShutdownTimeout sized to drain needs (30–60s for workers; K8s grace must exceed it). (6) Probes: fail readiness on stopping (stop receiving traffic while draining). Testing: start host, cancel token, assert drain completes + offsets persisted (integration test with short timeouts). What breaks it: synchronous blocking (Thread.Sleep — uncancellable), unobserved tasks (process exit mid-work), and Dispose-before-drain ordering (dispose after StopAsync completes).
internalWorking: ConsoleLifetime maps POSIX SIGTERM/Windows Ctrl events to ApplicationStopping (CancellationTokenSource.Cancel); HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout bounds StopAsync (default 5s — raise for drainers). K8s sends SIGTERM, waits terminationGracePeriodSeconds, then SIGKILL (uncatchable — drain must fit).
realWorldUsage: Deploy rollouts, pod evictions, autoscale-in, Windows service stops, and CI-killed workers.
commonMistake: Uncancellable awaits (hang to SIGKILL), abort-mid-batch (duplicates/loss without idempotency), no checkpointing (full restarts), and ShutdownTimeout left at 5s for 60s drains.
technicalConversation: Ask what happens to in-flight batches during their deploys — drain+checkpoint+idempotent (safe) versus abort (loss/dupes) is the maturity answer.
interviewFollowUp: Why must K8s terminationGracePeriodSeconds exceed the app's ShutdownTimeout?
keyTakeaway: Tokens everywhere, drain before exit, checkpoint always, idempotent applies. Size timeouts to drains.

questionText: How do ASP.NET Core health checks work, and how do you design liveness versus readiness probes?
shortAnswer: AddHealthChecks with check registrations → MapHealthChecks("/health") returning Healthy/Degraded/Unhealthy JSON. Liveness = process alive (cheap, rarely fails); readiness = ready for traffic (DB, deps, warmup done — fails during startup/drain). K8s restarts on liveness fail, stops traffic on readiness fail.
detailedAnswer: Registrations: AddCheck<DbCheck>("database", tags: new[] { "ready" }), AddUrlGroup (downstream), AddCheck<MemoryCheck> (self). Endpoints: /health/live (liveness: trivial — app responsive; Predicate _ => false with no checks, or a no-op check), /health/ready (Predicate r => r.Tags.Contains("ready"), checks DB/cache/downstream), /health (full detail for humans, auth-protected). ResponseWriter: UIResponseWriter (HealthChecks.UI format) or custom minimal JSON (status + per-check durations — duration spikes diagnose). Policies: failure status mapping (Unhealthy → 503), caching headers (no-cache), timeouts per check (a hung check must not hang the probe — CancellationToken + timeout). K8s: livenessProbe (restart loop-crashed), readinessProbe (remove from endpoints during startup/drain — initialDelaySeconds covers warmup; our seeder runs at startup — readiness must wait for it!), startupProbe (slow starters — disables liveness/readiness until first success). Custom checks implement IHealthCheck returning HealthCheckResult (Healthy/Unhealthy with data payloads — include versions/latency). Testing: hit endpoints in integration tests (200 + expected statuses), chaos (kill DB → readiness 503, liveness still 200).
internalWorking: HealthCheckService runs registered checks (parallel, cancellable) aggregating worst status; middleware maps to endpoint responses (predicate-filtered). Probes are plain HTTP GETs from kubelet (no auth by default — keep live/ready anonymous, protect detailed).
realWorldUsage: K8s deployments, load-balancer membership, deploy verification, and dependency dashboards.
commonMistake: One endpoint for both (restarts instead of traffic-shed), heavy checks on liveness (slow restarts), no startup probe for slow starters (kill loops during seeding/warmup!), and unauthenticated detailed endpoints (info leak).
technicalConversation: Ask what happens to their pods during a 60s migration/seeding at startup — without a startupProbe, liveness kills the pod mid-seed, forever.
interviewFollowUp: Why must readiness fail while liveness passes during graceful drain?
keyTakeaway: Live = alive, ready = traffic-worthy, startup = still warming. Probe each separately; protect detail.

questionText: What is the difference between PeriodicTimer, Task.Delay loops, and System.Threading.Timer?
shortAnswer: PeriodicTimer: modern async ticks (await WaitForNextTickAsync — no drift, cancellable, no reentrancy). Task.Delay loop: simple but drifts (work time adds) unless measured. Threading.Timer: callback-based (reentrancy risk, sync), legacy outside compat needs.
detailedAnswer: PeriodicTimer (preferred): var timer = new PeriodicTimer(interval); while (await timer.WaitForNextTickAsync(ct)) { work } — ticks align to schedule (no drift: long work skips missed ticks rather than bunching), cancellation via token (clean shutdown), no overlapping executions (ticks queue as booleans — one outstanding max), Dispose stops it. Task.Delay loop: while (!ct.IsCancellationRequested) { await Work(); await Task.Delay(interval, ct); } — drifts by work duration (add stopwatch compensation or accept it), simplest for irregular/conditional waits. System.Threading.Timer: callback on pool threads (reentrancy: slow callback + short period = overlapping runs — guard with change-due-time juggling or SemaphoreSlim), sync-only handlers (async void callbacks = unobserved death), IDisposable for stop (race-prone). Choice: periodic async work → PeriodicTimer; conditional/variable waits → Delay loop; legacy sync callbacks → Timer (with reentrancy guard). Precision: none guarantee real-time (15ms-ish OS granularity, pool delays) — need exactness? dedicated thread + spin (rare). Testing: abstract time (TimeProvider + FakeTimeProvider in .NET 8+: timer.WaitForNextTickAsync(fakeTime) deterministic — no Thread.Sleep in suites).
internalWorking: PeriodicTimer uses a single timer queue entry + ManualReset-style signaling (one waiter); WaitForNextTickAsync parks without threads. Task.Delay = timer + TaskCompletionSource (allocates per wait). Threading.Timer posts callbacks to the pool (overlap possible — no serialization).
realWorldUsage: Pollers, cache refreshers, heartbeat senders, metric flushers, and scheduled syncs.
commonMistake: Timer callback reentrancy (overlap corruption), Delay-loop drift treated as schedule (use PeriodicTimer), and Thread.Sleep in async code (blocks a pool thread — Delay instead).
technicalConversation: Ask whether their interval includes work time or not — Delay-loop (includes) versus PeriodicTimer (excludes/skips) is a scheduling-semantics decision.
interviewFollowUp: How do you unit test timer-driven code without waiting real time?
keyTakeaway: PeriodicTimer for ticks, Delay loops for conditional waits, Timer only for legacy sync. Abstract time in tests.

questionText: When should you use Quartz.NET or Hangfire instead of hand-rolled scheduling?
shortAnswer: Hand-roll single periodic loops (PeriodicTimer). Reach for Quartz (cron expressions, calendars, clustering, misfire policies) or Hangfire (persistent jobs, retries, dashboard, enqueue/defer/recurring) when schedules are complex, must survive restarts, or need observability.
detailedAnswer: Hand-rolled covers: fixed intervals, simple delays, in-memory only. Quartz.NET when: cron schedules (0 0 2 * * ?), calendars (exclude holidays), clustered singleton execution (DB-backed job store + locking — one node runs), misfire handling (late triggers: ignore/fire-now/coalesce policies), and job listeners (auditing). Hangfire when: fire-and-forget with persistence (enqueue survives restarts via storage), delayed jobs, recurring with dashboard (ops visibility: retries, failures, manual requeue), and continuations (ContinueJobWith chains). Storage matters: in-memory (dev/tests only — jobs vanish on restart), SQL Server/Postgres/Redis persistence (prod). Idempotency still required (at-least-once execution everywhere — retries + overlapping runs). Concurrency: DisableConcurrentExecution (Quartz) / DisableConcurrentExecution filter (Hangfire) for singleton jobs; distributed locks for hand-rolled multi-instance. Dashboard security: protect Hangfire UI (auth — it can requeue/delete jobs!). Our scope: PeriodicTimer suffices for pollers; document the Quartz/Hangfire threshold (cron complexity, persistence, multi-instance) so growth has a path.
internalWorking: Quartz stores triggers/jobs (RAMJobStore vs ADO stores with row locks for clustering); misfire checker threads apply policies. Hangfire persists job graphs (state machines: enqueued → processing → succeeded/failed with retry counters + exponential backoff) polled by servers.
realWorldUsage: Nightly reconciliations, scheduled reports, deferred emails/SMS, subscription renewals, and cleanup sweeps.
commonMistake: In-memory Hangfire in prod (jobs vanish on deploy), overlapping runs without locks (double charges!), cron without timezone specification (DST shifts — always set TimeZone), and unprotected dashboards (public job control).
technicalConversation: Ask what happens to Tuesday's 2am job during a deploy — persisted schedulers run it after (misfire policy); hand-rolled timers skip it silently.
interviewFollowUp: Why do scheduled jobs still need idempotency even with persistent schedulers?
keyTakeaway: Timers for loops, Quartz for cron/clustering, Hangfire for persistent jobs + dashboard. Idempotency everywhere regardless.

questionText: How do you use scoped services correctly inside singleton workers and middleware?
shortAnswer: Never inject scoped into singletons — inject IServiceScopeFactory (or IServiceProvider for factory use) and create a scope per unit of work. Middleware: use the endpoint's RequestServices scope (HttpContext.RequestServices), never root-resolved scoped instances.
detailedAnswer: Worker pattern: singleton BackgroundService takes IServiceScopeFactory; each tick/message creates using IServiceScope scope (fresh DbContext: no stale tracking, no cross-talk, disposed promptly). RequestServices: middleware/handlers resolve per-request scoped services from context.RequestServices (the framework scope — do not store them in fields!). Func<T>/Lazy<T> injection: deferred resolution still captures the creating scope (factory doesn't escape lifetime rules — resolve within the right scope). Common traps: constructor-injecting DbContext into a singleton (captive — stale + concurrency exceptions within hours under load), resolving scoped from root provider in Program.cs seeding (create scope explicitly — our seeder does), Blazor Server circuits (scoped = circuit lifetime, much longer than HTTP — same discipline, longer horizon), and Parallel.ForEach sharing one scoped DbContext (DbContext is NOT thread-safe — scope per partition). Validation: ValidateScopes in dev/test catches these at resolve time (enable always). Review rule: singleton ctors contain only singletons + factories; everything else is a bug until proven otherwise.
internalWorking: Scopes are nested service caches (child of root or parent); disposal cascades (scope dispose → disposes its IDisposables). RequestServices scope lives for the request; worker-created scopes live for the using block. Root resolution of scoped throws with validation (or silently captions without it — the dangerous default in prod without validation!).
realWorldUsage: Workers, middleware tenant resolution, Blazor circuits, parallel partition processing, and startup seeding.
commonMistake: DbContext in singleton ctor (the classic production incident), stored RequestServices resolutions (stale across requests), Parallel sharing one context (thread-safety violation), and no ValidateScopes (silent capture in prod).
technicalConversation: Ask to see a singleton's constructor in their codebase right now — every non-singleton parameter gets the factory-or-scope interrogation.
interviewFollowUp: Why is DbContext not thread-safe, and what breaks when Parallel shares one?
keyTakeaway: Singletons take factories; units of work take scopes. RequestServices per request, never stored.

questionText: How do container liveness and readiness probes use health endpoints in practice (with YAML)?
shortAnswer: Map /health/live (trivial) + /health/ready (deps) in the app; reference them from deployment YAML with staggered delays (startup covers seeding/warmup, readiness gates traffic, liveness restarts deadlocks). Tune periods/thresholds to failure costs, not defaults.
detailedAnswer: Wiring: app exposes the two endpoints (previous question); K8s calls them. YAML shape: startupProbe (httpGet /health/ready... actually startup usually hits ready-or-live with long failureThreshold: periodSeconds 10, failureThreshold 30 = 5min warmup budget covering migrations+seeding+JIT warmup), readinessProbe (period 10s, failureThreshold 3 → 30s to shed traffic; successThreshold 1 to rejoin), livenessProbe (period 30s, failureThreshold 3 → restart after 90s truly dead; NEVER aggressive liveness — restarts lose in-flight work and cascade). Our app specifics: seeding runs at startup (tens of seconds with 500+ questions eventually) — startupProbe must cover it or pods die mid-seed forever (CrashLoopBackOff that looks like an app bug!). Numbers: initialDelaySeconds 0 with startupProbe (don't double-delay), timeoutSeconds 5 (hung checks fail fast), terminationGracePeriodSeconds > app ShutdownTimeout (60s grace vs 30s drain). Docker Compose: healthcheck test CMD-SHELL wget + interval/retries/start_period mirrors (start_period covers seeding). Compose/Swarm/compose-prod parity keeps local honest. Verification: kill -STOP the process (liveness should fire, readiness first), block the DB (readiness 503, liveness 200 — traffic sheds, pod lives), and deploy during seeding (startupProbe absorbs it).
codeExample:
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /health/live, port: 8080 }
  periodSeconds: 30
  failureThreshold: 3
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /health/ready, port: 8080 }
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 3
startupProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /health/ready, port: 8080 }
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 36  # 6 min for migrations + seeding + warmup
internalWorking: Kubelet GETs the endpoint (no auth by default — keep probes anonymous); consecutive failures past threshold trigger actions (restart vs endpoint-removal). Startup probe success disables itself and enables the other two. terminationGrace: SIGTERM → grace → SIGKILL (align with app drain).
realWorldUsage: Every containerized .NET deployment, Compose health gating (depends_on condition), and LB target health.
commonMistake: No startupProbe with slow seeding (crash-loop that mimics app bugs!), aggressive liveness (restart storms), one endpoint for both (restarts instead of shed), and grace < drain (SIGKILL mid-batch).
technicalConversation: Ask what covers their seeding window — nothing (crash-loops on first big seed) versus startupProbe (boring deploys) is the whole story.
interviewFollowUp: Why does an aggressive liveness probe cause cascading outages while a slow one merely delays recovery?
keyTakeaway: Startup covers warmup, readiness sheds traffic, liveness restarts the dead. Size every number from real timings.

questionText: How do you run .NET as a Windows Service or systemd daemon, and what changes versus console hosting?
shortAnswer: Add UseWindowsService()/UseSystemd() — one call each fixing content-root, lifetime (Service Control Manager/systemd signals), event-log/systemd logging, and restart policies. The rest (config, DI, workers) is identical; differences live in deployment (install/publish profiles) and observability (journal/event log).
detailedAnswer: Windows: .UseWindowsService() (Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting.WindowsServices) — sets content root to the exe dir (services start in System32 otherwise — config/files break without this!), wires SCM start/stop to host lifetime, logs to Event Log provider (add .AddEventLog()). Install: sc.exe create (binPath, start=auto, obj credentials) or installer/MSIX; publish single-file friendly. systemd: .UseSystemd() — content root likewise, SIGTERM→lifetime mapping, journal logging (console provider suffices — journal captures stdout with priorities via syslog identifiers), notify readiness (Type=notify + systemd-notify integration in .NET 8+: SD_NOTIFY ready right after host start — accurate readiness vs sleep-guessing). Unit file: Restart=always + RestartSec backoff, User= least-privilege, WorkingDirectory, EnvironmentFile for secrets (0600), StartLimit* anti-spam. Differences from console: no interactive stdin/Console.ReadKey (gate behind Environment.UserInteractive), paths must be absolute-or-content-rooted (never CWD-relative — our technical_mastery.db relative path is a dev-only convenience; prod uses absolute data dir!), and stdout buffering in journals (flush or line-buffer). Updates: stop-replace-start (downtime) vs side-by-side + proxy cutover (zero-downtime) vs containers (replace image).
internalWorking: WindowsServiceLifetime intercepts SCM callbacks (OnStart → host StartAsync; OnStop → StopAsync with SCM timeout ~30s default — raise via ServicesPipeTimeout for long drains). SystemdLifetime maps SIGTERM/SIGRTMIN (reload) similarly; Type=notify support signals READY=1 post-start (accurate probe-less readiness).
realWorldUsage: On-prem agents, factory-floor collectors, Windows back-office services, and Linux edge daemons.
commonMistake: CWD-relative paths (services start in System32/ — files 'vanish'), Console.ReadKey blocking headless start (gate it), SCM 30s stop timeout vs 60s drains (lost work — raise or drain faster), and journal absence planning (no log files on box — journalctl is the interface).
technicalConversation: Ask where their service writes files — CWD-relative paths are the classic works-on-dev-dies-as-service bug.
interviewFollowUp: Why must content-root be set explicitly for services, and what breaks without it?
keyTakeaway: One call per OS for lifetime+paths+logs. Absolute paths, no console reads, journal/event-log observability.

questionText: How do you achieve zero-downtime deployments for .NET APIs (slots, rolling, blue-green)?
shortAnswer: Never stop-then-start in place: run new version alongside (slot/staging pod set), warm it (health + seeded + JIT-warmed), shift traffic (swap/split), watch, rollback by shifting back. Database compatibility (expand-then-contract migrations) is the actual hard part — app swapping is easy.
detailedAnswer: Patterns: (1) Slots (App Service): staging slot warms (startupProbe equivalent: applicationInitialization), swap VIP (instant cutover, instant swap-back rollback). Slot-specific settings (connection strings sticky to prod — rehearse!). (2) Rolling (K8s Deployment): maxSurge/maxUnavailable bound disruption (25% defaults sane), readiness gates each pod (traffic only to warm), old pods drain (SIGTERM + preStop sleep for LB deregistration lag). (3) Blue-green: two full stacks + router flip (DNS/LB weight), instant rollback, double cost during switch. (4) Canary: 1–5% traffic to new (metrics compared — error/latency burn decides promotion). The DB problem: new code + old schema and old code + new schema must BOTH work during transition → expand migrations (add nullable columns/tables first, deploy code using them, later contract: drop old) — never rename/drop in the same deploy as code use. Backward/forward checks in CI (migration compatibility tests). In-flight work: drain on SIGTERM (previous question), sticky sessions (avoid — design stateless; where unavoidable, drain-aware). Verification: synthetic transactions post-shift, error-budget burn alerts (auto-rollback on burn), and rehearsed rollback (rollback tested = rollback trusted).
internalWorking: Swap = router pointer change (atomic at LB); rolling = replica-set scaling with readiness gating per pod; canary = weighted routing (service mesh percentages). Expand-contract keeps both schema versions queryable (nullable adds are backward compatible; drops are not).
realWorldUsage: Production API deploys, migration-heavy releases, and multi-region rollouts.
commonMistake: Breaking schema + code in one deploy (mixed-version outage), no preStop sleep (in-flight 502s during drain), sticky-slot settings untested (staging works, swapped prod breaks), and canary without auto-rollback (eyeballs don't scale).
technicalConversation: Ask how their last migration deployed — expand-contract with traffic shifting (safe) versus stop-migrate-start (downtime they may not have noticed).
interviewFollowUp: Why must database changes lead app changes by one deploy, and what breaks when they ship together?
keyTakeaway: Shift traffic, never stop in place. Expand-then-contract schemas; drain, gate, and rehearse rollback.
